body.text: In Canada, recapture of investment tax credit under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the Income Tax Act adds an amount, capped at the SR&ED investment tax credit earned, to Part I tax payable when property that earned the credit in the preceding 20 taxation years is sold, converted to commercial use or disposed of to a non-arm's length party.

This report provides a technical audit and legal analysis of the Research and Development (R&D) tax incentive framework, grant ecosystem, administrative compliance procedures, and judicial jurisprudence of Canada as of November 2026.

Canada's flagship R&D fiscal mechanism—the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program—underwent its most significant legislative overhaul in over a decade between December 2024 and October 2026. Enacted via Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, and effective retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the federal reforms doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3 million to $6 million (yielding up to $2.1 million in annual refundable credits), expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended the 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out ($15 million–$75 million), and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Concurrently, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process on April 1, 2026, providing upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks and halving post-filing expenditure review service standards from 180 days to 90 days. At the provincial level, Québec replaced its legacy R&D and innovation tax measures with the consolidated Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, offering a 30% refundable credit on the first $1 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures (above an exclusion threshold) and 20% thereafter.

Practitioners and corporate claimants must also correct three persistent technical errors that frequently trigger CRA audit reassessments. First, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under the proxy method is 55% of the eligible salary base pursuant to subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations—not 65%, which has not applied since 2012. Second, as highlighted in practitioner audit guidance, cloud computing and Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) infrastructure expenses cannot be claimed separately under the proxy method; they are covered by the notional 55% PPA and can only be claimed as actual, directly related, and incremental overhead expenditures if the taxpayer elects the traditional method. Third, the statutory SR&ED reporting deadline under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act (18 months after the taxation year-end for corporations) is an absolute bar that cannot be waived or extended under the taxpayer relief provisions of subsection 220(2.2).
1. Legislative Architecture and the 2024–2026 Statutory Reforms
1.1 Dual Statutory Pillars: Section 37 and Section 127 of the Income Tax Act

The federal SR&ED program is co-administered by the Department of Finance Canada, which formulates legislative tax policy, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which executes technical and financial compliance reviews. Under the Income Tax Act (ITA), R&D tax incentives operate through a bifurcated statutory mechanism that requires two related but legally distinct calculations.

The first calculation determines the Section 37 Deduction Pool. Subsection 37(1) establishes a cumulative pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada that relate to a business carried on by the taxpayer (or a related corporation actively engaged in that business at the time the expenditure is incurred, pursuant to subsection 37(1.1)). Taxpayers may deduct any portion of their available Section 37 pool balance against net business income in the current taxation year or carry the undeducted balance forward indefinitely to offset business income in future taxation years. Research carried on outside Canada is governed separately by subsection 37(2), which permits a current-year income deduction for current expenditures incurred outside Canada (while subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) allow a restricted portion of permissible foreign salaries into the Section 37(1) pool), but research outside Canada generally does not generate Investment Tax Credits except on those permissible salaries.

The second calculation determines Qualified Expenditures and Investment Tax Credits under Section 127 and Section 127.1. Subsections 127(5) and 127(9) govern the calculation of "qualified expenditures" and the earning of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits to offset federal Part I tax otherwise payable. Section 127.1 (specifically subsections 127.1(1), 127.1(2), and 127.1(2.01)) governs the calculation of the "refundable investment tax credit," allowing eligible entities to receive direct cash refunds for unused ITCs after reducing Part I tax payable to zero.

A foundational audit rule is that "deductible SR&ED expenditure" under section 37 and "qualified expenditure" under subsection 127(9) are not interchangeable statutory concepts. Certain outlays—such as non-arm's length SR&ED subcontracts where no Form T1146 transfer agreement is filed, or acquisitions of used depreciable capital property after December 15, 2024—are deductible in computing the Section 37 expenditure pool but are statutorily excluded from earning an ITC under section 127 and section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations. Conversely, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) calculated under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations is a notional addition included solely in the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool to generate ITCs, and is never added to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool. Furthermore, under paragraph 37(1)(e), any federal SR&ED ITC claimed (whether used to offset Part I tax or received as a cash refund) in a given taxation year reduces the taxpayer's Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the immediately following taxation year (or in the same fiscal period for partnerships).
1.2 Chronology of the 2024–2026 Federal Legislative Reforms (Bill C-15)

Following the Department of Finance Canada's two-phase SR&ED consultation launched in 2024, the federal government enacted comprehensive legislative modernizations across three sequential policy instruments. First, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (released December 16, 2024) and the Department of Finance's Draft Legislative Proposals (released August 15, 2025) initially proposed increasing the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC from $3 million to $4.5 million (yielding a maximum $1.575 million refundable credit), raising the CCPC prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extending the enhanced 35% ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), introducing an elective gross revenue phase-out structure, and restoring the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment leases incurred after December 15, 2024.

Second, in Federal Budget 2025 (presented on November 4, 2025 by the Minister of Finance and National Revenue, the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne), the federal government confirmed the 2024 Fall Economic Statement architecture and further increased the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC from the proposed $4.5 million to $6 million (yielding up to $2.1 million per year in refundable ITCs on current expenditures), effective retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Third, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, codifying the $6 million expenditure limit, ECPC eligibility, the $15 million–$75 million phase-out ranges, and the restoration of capital and lease expenditures into the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations. Separately, Federal Budget 2026 (tabled November 5, 2026) proposes, for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026, to extend SR&ED eligibility to tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements for obtaining the initial approval or certification necessary to commercialize a product or process, and to costs of registering and maintaining intellectual property protection for intellectual property developed in an eligible SR&ED project (with recapture of the related SR&ED deduction and ITC on a disposition of that intellectual property); these measures are proposals and have not been enacted.

body.text: 2. Scientific and Technological Eligibility Criteria
2.1 Statutory Definition Under Subsection 248(1)

The gateway to all federal and harmonized provincial R&D incentives is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls into one of four permitted statutory categories.

Under paragraph (a), eligible work includes basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Under paragraph (b), eligible work includes applied research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view (for example, laboratory efforts to develop a vaccine against a newly discovered virus by exploiting its identified biological characteristics). Under paragraph (c), which accounts for the vast majority of Canadian corporate claims, eligible work includes experimental development, defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements. Finally, under paragraph (d), SR&ED includes support work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight enumerated disciplines—engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada.
2.2 The CRA "Why" and "How" Framework vs. The Five Jurisprudential Questions

On August 13, 2021, the CRA archived its former Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy and issued the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. The 2021 Guidelines distil the subsection 248(1) definition into two mandatory requirements—the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement—that must both be met for work to qualify.

The "Why" Requirement mandates that work be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving technological advancement. This requires generating or discovering conceptual knowledge (such as theories, predictive models, or an understanding of how constituents are embodied and interact within a material, device, product, or process) rather than routine factual knowledge (such as simple measurements or data points). New knowledge is required only when a scientific or technological uncertainty exists—meaning whether or how a given objective or result can be achieved is unknown and cannot be determined on the basis of the combined knowledge and experience available within the business and in publicly accessible sources. Recognising scientific or technological uncertainty marks the starting point of SR&ED, and seeking advancement to resolve that uncertainty is the targeted outcome. Common indicators of insufficient technological knowledge include situations where existing design methods are inapplicable, requirements or specifications conflict with established standards, excessive variables or interlocking constraints exist, operating parameters fall outside normal ranges, data is not readily available, the nature of the problem is evolving, or "system uncertainty" arises from unpredictable interactions when integrating known sub-systems. Success or failure in achieving the commercial or technical objective is irrelevant, as the statute requires only that the purpose of the work is to achieve advancement. While pure economic constraints or cost targets alone do not constitute technological uncertainty, attempting to achieve technical performance within rigid cost targets can impose genuine technological uncertainty.

The "How" Requirement mandates that the work be carried out as a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Merely conducting work in an organized or systematic manner is insufficient. Rather, the systematic investigation must begin by generating an idea or hypothesis consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for resolving the technological uncertainty. The claimant must then test that hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis (recognising that the hypothesis may evolve and be modified as testing progresses), develop logical conclusions based on the experimental or analytical findings, and keep contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses.

Crucially, as the CRA acknowledges in its guidance history and as the Tax Court of Canada and Federal Court of Appeal consistently hold, the "Why" and "How" requirements are derived from the exact same statutory definition in subsection 248(1) as the five foundational questions established by Chief Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC) and adopted by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393:

items: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?
Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?
Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?
Did the process result in a technological advancement?
Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results kept as the work progressed?

3. Federal Tax Credit Rates, Expenditure Limits, Phase-Outs, and Carryforwards
3.1 Entity Classifications, Credit Rates, and Refundability Matrix

Under subsections 127(5), 127(9), 127(10.1), and section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, the rate at which a claimant earns SR&ED ITCs and the proportion of unused ITCs that can be refunded in cash depend on the legal status of the taxpayer, the nature of the expenditure (current vs. capital), and whether the expenditure falls within the annual expenditure limit.

Qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs)—defined as CCPCs (that are not excluded corporations) whose prior-year taxable income combined across their associated corporate group does not exceed their qualifying income limit—earn the enhanced 35% ITC on qualified expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit ($6 million for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024). Unused 35% ITCs earned on current expenditures are 100% refundable (generating up to $2.1 million in annual cash refunds), while unused 35% ITCs earned on capital expenditures (for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024) are 40% refundable. For qualified expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit, a qualifying CCPC earns the basic 15% ITC, which is 40% refundable on both current and capital expenditures.

For CCPCs that are "Excluded Corporations" (under subsection 127.1(2)), the corporation earns the 35% ITC up to its expenditure limit and 15% above the limit, with a 40% refundability rate across both current and capital expenditures. By contrast, CCPCs other than qualifying or excluded corporations (i.e., CCPCs whose prior-year associated taxable income exceeds their qualifying income limit, but that still retain an expenditure limit under the taxable capital or gross revenue phase-out tests) earn the 35% ITC up to their expenditure limit (100% refundable on current expenditures and 40% refundable on capital expenditures), but their 15% ITC earned on expenditures over the expenditure limit is 0% refundable (non-refundable).

Effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) also gain access to the enhanced refundable credit regime. Under subsection 127(9), an ECPC is defined as a corporation that, throughout the taxation year: (1) is resident in Canada; (2) has a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or has elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation); and (3) is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons (or is a Canadian-resident corporation where all or substantially all of the shares of its capital stock are owned by one or more ECPCs). Under amended subsection 127.1(2.01), ECPCs earn the enhanced 35% ITC up to the $6 million expenditure limit, with 100% refundability on current expenditures and 40% refundability on capital expenditures. Expenditures exceeding the ECPC's expenditure limit earn the 15% basic ITC, which is non-refundable (0%).

All other corporations (such as foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries and large public corporations above the $75 million phase-out threshold) earn the 15% non-refundable ITC on all qualified current and capital expenditures. Finally, individuals, unincorporated businesses, certain trusts, and members of a partnership earn the 15% basic ITC, which is 40% refundable on both current and capital expenditures. Under subsection 127(8), a partnership calculates its SR&ED ITC solely at the 15% basic rate, even if its partners are CCPCs; furthermore, no SR&ED ITC may be allocated to a "specified member" of a partnership (such as a limited partner or passive general partner), and any unallocated specified member ITCs must either be reallocated to active general partners or renounced using Form T932 under subsection 127(8.4).

C. Short Taxation Years and Associated/Consolidated Group Allocations

If a corporation's taxation year is less than 51 weeks, its annual expenditure limit must be prorated by multiplying the calculated expenditure limit by the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year to 365. For example, as illustrated in the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026), if an associated group allocates the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit to Corporation X for a 273-day short taxation year in 2026, Corporation X's prorated expenditure limit is $6,000,000 × (273 / 365) = $4,487,671 (compared to $3,000,000 × (273 / 365) = $2,243,836 under the pre-December 16, 2024 rules).

Associated CCPCs must allocate the annual expenditure limit among group members using Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit, updated May 29, 2026) under subsection 127(10.3). For consolidated ECPCs (defined via "consolidated financial statements" under subsection 233.8(1)) or CCPCs electing the revenue method, allocation falls under subsections 127(10.6) and 127(10.62). If an associated or consolidated group fails to file an allocation agreement within 30 days of a CRA request, the Minister may allocate the expenditure limit under subsections 127(10.4) and 127(10.64).
3.3 Carryback, Carryforward, and Loss Restriction Event Rules

Unused non-refundable SR&ED Investment Tax Credits earned under section 127 may be carried back 3 taxation years (to reduce federal Part I tax payable in those preceding years) and carried forward up to 20 taxation years. Conversely, a positive balance in the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures does not expire and can be carried forward indefinitely as a running balance to offset business income in future taxation years. Because a partnership is not a separate person for tax purposes, partnerships cannot carry forward any amount in the Section 37 pool to subsequent years; under paragraph 96(1)(e.1), the entire Section 37 pool balance must be deducted in computing the partnership's net income for the fiscal period, and any partnership loss created or increased by claiming the Section 37 pool is disallowed to limited partners.

When a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control (or a trust acquires a new majority-interest beneficiary), a loss restriction event occurs, triggering a deemed taxation year-end immediately before the event and reducing the Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool to nil under paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1). Consequential on the restoration of capital expenditures in Bill C-15, clause 37(6.1)(a)(i)(B) was amended to ensure these loss restriction rules apply equally to capital property described in paragraph 37(1)(b) acquired on or after December 16, 2024. Following a loss restriction event, the undeducted prior pool balance is reinstated and deductible in a subsequent taxation year only if: (1) the specific business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit throughout that subsequent year; and (2) the deduction is limited to the net income for that taxation year derived from that same business or a similar business (computed before claiming the SR&ED pool deduction).
4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Overhead Calculation Methods
4.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method Election

Under clauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) and subsection 37(10) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant must select either the Traditional Method or the Proxy Method to compute SR&ED expenditures for each taxation year on Form T661. The selection is made on a year-by-year basis; while a claimant may change methods from one taxation year to the next, the choice made when first filing Form T661 for a given taxation year is irrevocable for that year. If a claimant does not elect the proxy method on Form T661, the traditional method applies automatically.

body.text: 4.2 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees, and YMPE Caps

Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), eligible labour costs are restricted to salaries or wages as defined in subsection 248(1) (income from an office or employment computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I, reported on T4 slips) incurred and paid in the taxation year or within 180 days after the end of the taxation year. Under subsections 143.3(3) and 143.3(5), stock option benefits are not expenditures incurred by the employer and are excluded. Extended vacation or sick leave, retiring allowances (under the proxy method), and the notional value of non-cash taxable benefits under section 6 (where no actual cash outlay is incurred by the employer) are also excluded from SR&ED salary and wages. Furthermore, salaries or drawings paid to sole proprietors or partners of an unincorporated business are not employment income and cannot be claimed.
A. Specified Employees vs. Employees Other Than Specified Employees

Subsection 248(1) defines a "specified employee" of a taxpayer as an employee who is a specified shareholder of the taxpayer (owning, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation) or who does not deal at arm's length with the taxpayer under section 251. Specified employees are subject to two separate statutory caps depending on whether the calculation is for the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool or the Proxy Method salary base.

First, for the Section 37 Deductible Pool and Direct Wage Calculation (5x YMPE Rule) under subsections 37(9) and 37(9.1) of the Income Tax Act, all bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee are 100% excluded from allowable SR&ED salary or wages. (The sole administrative exception under section 4.0 of the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy applies where a specified employee's only remuneration for performing SR&ED duties consists of a bonus or profit-based remuneration and all required payroll deductions were remitted, in which case the CRA treats an amount commensurate with those duties as regular salary or wages.) In addition, the maximum allowable SR&ED salary or wages claimed for a specified employee cannot exceed 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days the individual was a specified employee in the taxation year. If a specified employee performs SR&ED for two or more associated corporations, no amount may be claimed unless the associated corporations allocate the 5x YMPE limit using Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) filed by each corporation's reporting deadline.

Second, for the Proxy Method Salary Base Calculation (75% and 2.5x YMPE Rule) under subsections 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(9) of the Income Tax Regulations, the salary base used to compute the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount excludes bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, employer-paid related benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the current year (Line 310 of Form T661) for all employees. For a specified employee, the amount included in the PPA salary base is further restricted to the lesser of: (1) the specified employee's eligible base salary multiplied by the percentage of time spent directly engaged in SR&ED, capped at 75% of total eligible salary; and (2) 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated for the number of days the claimant employed the individual in the taxation year:
Specified Employee PPA Salary Base = lesser of (eligible salary × % of time directly engaged in SR&ED, up to 75% × total eligible salary) and (2.5 × A × B ÷ 365)
where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual.

Note that under subsection 2900(7), there is no proration for the portion of the year the employee was not a specified employee. Under subsections 2900(8) and 2900(10), if a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations (including deemed associated individuals or partnerships) in taxation years ending in the same calendar year, the combined PPA salary base across the associated group cannot exceed 2.5 times the YMPE.
B. YMPE Caps for 2023–2027

Although the Canada Pension Plan introduced a second earnings ceiling in 2024—the Year's Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YAMPE) for CPP2 contributions—the statutory SR&ED caps in subsection 37(9.1) of the Income Tax Act and subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) of the Income Tax Regulations remain legally tied to the first earnings ceiling (YMPE) under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan.

body.text: C. All or Substantially All (90%) Labour Rule and Permissible Foreign Salaries (10% Rule)

Under subsection 2900(5) of the Income Tax Regulations and sections 7.3.4 and 8.3.3 of the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, if an employee spends all or substantially all (90% or more) of their working time throughout the taxation year directly engaged in (under the proxy method) or undertaking, supervising, or supporting (under the traditional method) SR&ED in Canada, 100% of that employee's eligible salary or wages is included in the SR&ED claim (subject to the 75% and 2.5x YMPE cap for specified employees in the proxy salary base). Under section 7.1.1 of the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, tasks performed by non-specialized employees (such as operating a machine required for an experiment or feeding raw materials into a test line) also qualify as "directly engaged" labour if the work directly supports and is an integral part of the SR&ED and is supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications.

Under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the Income Tax Act, salaries and wages paid to employees for SR&ED work performed outside Canada qualify for inclusion in the Section 37(1) pool, the PPA salary base, and the Section 127 ITC calculation if three statutory conditions are met: (1) the foreign SR&ED work is solely in support of SR&ED carried on by the taxpayer inside Canada; (2) the salary or wages are not subject to an income or profits tax imposed by another country; and (3) the total permissible foreign SR&ED salary claimed (allocated on Form T661 between Line 307 for non-specified employees and Line 309 for specified employees) does not exceed 10% of the total eligible SR&ED salaries and wages incurred for work performed inside Canada (reported on Line 306 of Form T661):
Line 307 + Line 309 ≤ 10% × Line 306
4.3 Prescribed Proxy Amount (55% Rate), Overall Cap, and Cloud Computing Rules
A. Correcting the Proxy Rate Misconception (55% vs. 65%)

Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is 55% of the salary base. A widespread error in secondary commentary is citing a 65% or 60% proxy rate; in law, the 65% rate applied only up to 2012, decreased to 60% for 2013, and has been fixed at 55% since 2014. Furthermore, under subsection 2900(6) of the Income Tax Regulations, the PPA is subject to an Overall Cap ensuring that total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and specific statutory deductions do not exceed total business operating deductions claimed in the year:
PPA ≤ A − B − C

where A is total amounts deducted in computing net business income for tax purposes for the year (including cost of goods sold), B is the sum of deductions claimed under sections 20 (including Capital Cost Allowance, interest, and bad debts), 24, 26, 30, 32, 37 (SR&ED deduction), 66–66.8, and 104, and C is any expenditure incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building. As noted in the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy (updated March 27, 2026), this cap generally does not restrict the PPA if the claimant deducted more than $55 of non-SR&ED operating expenses for every $100 of eligible salary in the salary base.
B. Audit Treatment of Cloud Computing (AWS/Azure/GCP), Software, and Bandwidth

For data analytics, software, and artificial intelligence firms, the treatment of cloud computing and software costs depends directly on the overhead method election. As emphasized in CPA practitioner audit warnings, cloud computing infrastructure (such as AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud compute instances) and software subscriptions are classified as overhead / current service expenditures, not materials. Under the Proxy Method, actual overhead expenses are not identified or claimed at all because the notional 55% PPA stands in for them; claiming cloud computing invoices under the proxy method results in automatic audit disallowance. Conversely, under the Traditional Method, actual cloud computing expenses are claimable on Line 360 of Form T661 if they are itemized and proven to be directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED under paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Income Tax Regulations. For compute-intensive teams where incremental cloud spend exceeds 55% of the salary base, electing the traditional method yields a higher deduction and ITC.

With respect to software and software licences, section 4.2 of the CRA's SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026) and section 5 of the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026) clarify that software and software user licences are intangible property rather than leased equipment. Software intended to be incorporated into a commercial product cannot be included in the Section 37 pool. However, software acquired after December 15, 2024 strictly as a tool for performing SR&ED (such as computer-aided design or simulation software) qualifies for the Section 37 pool as a current expenditure (if it benefits only the current fiscal period) or as a capital expenditure (if its useful life endures beyond one year and it meets the ≥90% ASA test). Furthermore, under section 4.3.1 of the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024 for leasing internet bandwidth used in SR&ED in Canada explicitly qualify as equipment lease costs under both the traditional method and the proxy method, provided the ≥90% ASA or >50% primary usage criteria are met.
4.4 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's Length Transfers, and Third-Party Payments
A. Arm's-Length vs. Non-Arm's Length SR&ED Contracts

When a claimant contracts out SR&ED work to be performed on its behalf in Canada under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), the claimant must separate arm's-length and non-arm's length contractors. For arm's-length Canadian contractors (who must be a "taxable supplier"—defined in subsection 127(9) as a person resident in Canada, a Canadian partnership, or a non-resident operating through a permanent establishment in Canada under section 8201 of the Regulations), 100% of the eligible contract amount is deductible in the Section 37 pool, and 80% of the eligible contract expenditure qualifies for the Section 127 ITC. Consequential on Bill C-15's addition of paragraph 37(1)(b), subsection 37(14) (the contract look-through rule) was repealed for property acquired and lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024; accordingly, payers are no longer required to reduce contract expenditures or third-party payments by capital expenditures incurred by the performer.

For non-arm's length (NAL) contractors, payments are deductible in the payer's Section 37 pool, but do not qualify for an ITC in the hands of the payer unless the performer (transferor) and payer (transferee) execute and file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026) to transfer the performer's qualified expenditures (including its PPA) to the payer. Furthermore, where an SR&ED performer purchases goods or non-SR&ED services from a NAL supplier, subsections 127(11.6) and 127(11.7) restrict the performer's qualified expenditure to the NAL supplier's "adjusted selling cost" or "adjusted service cost", stripping out any inter-company profit.
B. Third-Party Payments (Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii))

Under the Third-Party Payments Policy (updated March 30, 2022), third-party payments are distinguished from SR&ED contracts because the performer controls the SR&ED work (typically basic or applied research), multiple funders usually contribute, and the claimant obtains a non-exclusive, preferential right to exploit the results in a business it carries on. Third-party payments are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool and 80% eligible for ITCs, must be reported on Form T1263, and apply to six entity categories: Entity A (Canadian-resident corporations under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1), claimed on an accrual basis in the year the SR&ED is performed) and Entities B through F (approved associations, approved universities/colleges/research institutes, non-profit SR&ED corporations exempt under paragraph 149(1)(j), and approved granting councils under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(ii) and (iii), all claimed on a cash basis in the year payment is made). Agricultural producers contributing via check-off dues to agricultural organizations that fund approved B, C, or D entities may also earn ITCs on the SR&ED-allocated portion of their contributions.
C. Unpaid Amounts (180-Day Rule Under Subsections 78(4) and 127(26))

Two statutory 180-day unpaid amount rules govern timing on Form T661. Under subsection 78(4), salary or wages incurred in a taxation year that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in that year; they are only added to the Section 37 pool and eligible for ITCs in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid (and under Regulation 2900(9), prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year on Line 310 are permanently excluded from the Proxy Method salary base). Under subsection 127(26), other current expenditures (such as SR&ED contract payables or materials) that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year remain deductible in the Section 37 pool when incurred, but are excluded from "qualified expenditures" for ITC purposes until the taxation year in which they are paid.
4.5 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed, Production Runs, and Recapture

Under the Materials for SR&ED Policy and SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy, materials (purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers) used directly in SR&ED in Canada are claimable under both the traditional and proxy methods if they are either materials consumed (destroyed or rendered virtually valueless, retaining ≤10% of their original cost; if ≥90% ASA of a material's cost is consumed in SR&ED, 100% is allowable) or materials transformed (incorporated into another material, prototype, or product while retaining a value >10% of original cost). While general utilities (electricity, fuel, boiler/utility water) are overhead claimable only under the traditional method, energy directly input into endothermic reactions (where intermediate or final products retain the energy in a new physical or chemical form) and process feed water that becomes chemically part of an intermediate or final product qualify as materials consumed under both methods.

When experimental development occurs during manufacturing production runs (SR&ED During Production Runs Policy), the CRA distinguishes between two contexts. In an Experimental Development + Experimental Production (ED+EP) context (such as operating a dedicated pilot plant or a production run with documented technical risk of process instability, equipment damage, or yield loss), full direct labour and materials consumed or transformed in the required run are allowable (excluding excess production). In an Experimental Development + Commercial Production (ED+CP) context (where experimental development occurs simultaneously alongside commercial production), normal commercial production costs are excluded and only the additional (incremental) labour and material costs attributable to the experimental development are allowable. Where it is impractical to apportion costs between SR&ED and commercial work while developing a custom product or commercial asset, the CRA permits an Alternative Approach: total actual development costs minus the estimated normal construction cost had the technology already existed, plus estimated materials transformed.

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) (Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy), if a property that incorporates transformed materials, property acquired via an SR&ED contract, SR&ED capital property, or shared-use equipment on which an ITC was earned in any of the 20 preceding taxation years is sold (recaptured on proceeds of disposition) or converted to commercial use / disposed of to a non-arm's length party (recaptured on fair market value), the lesser of the original ITC earned on the property and the original ITC rate (15% or 35%) applied to the proceeds/FMV is added to Part I tax payable in the year of sale or conversion. Under paragraph 37(1)(c.2), any recaptured ITC added to Part I tax payable increases the claimant's Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the subsequent taxation year.
4.6 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)
A. Restored SR&ED Capital Expenditures (Paragraph 37(1)(b))

Under the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026) and Bill C-15, expenditures made after December 15, 2024 to acquire new or used depreciable property (as defined in subsection 13(21) of the ITA, once "available for use" under subsection 37(1.2)) qualify for 100% inclusion in the Section 37 deductible pool (claimed on Line 390 and Part 6B of Form T661, rather than on CCA Schedule T2SCH8) if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended that the property would either: (1) be used during all or substantially all (≥90% ASA) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada; or (2) have all or substantially all (≥90% ASA) of its value consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada.

Two critical statutory exclusions govern capital claims. First, under paragraph 2902(b) of the Income Tax Regulations, while depreciable property that was used prior to acquisition (or refurbished used property) can be deducted in the Section 37 pool if it satisfies the ≥90% ASA intent test, used property is excluded from "qualified expenditures" and earns 0% ITC. Second, under paragraphs 37(8)(d) and 37(8)(e), non-depreciable property (land, inventory, goodwill) and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings are excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures, except for a prescribed special-purpose building approved on a building-by-building basis by the Department of Finance Canada under section 2903 of the Income Tax Regulations. If SR&ED capital property is later sold, Line 440 of Form T661 reduces the Section 37 pool by the lesser of the proceeds of disposition and the undeducted pool balance for that property, while any excess proceeds up to the original capital cost trigger CCA recapture on Schedule T2SCH1 (in addition to ITC recapture on Schedule T2SCH31).
B. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) vs. Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP)

Under the SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026) and subsection 127(9), new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the ≥90% ASA test—and is not General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF)—qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) if it is actually used primarily (>50% but <90% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada. The capital cost of SUE is not deductible in the Section 37 pool and must be depreciated via regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) on Schedule T2SCH8. However, under both the traditional and proxy methods, 25% (1/4) of the capital cost qualifies for an ITC on Line 504 (and Part 6C) of Form T661 as First-Term SUE (where actual SR&ED operating time is >50% in the first period running from when the asset becomes available for use to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months later), and an additional 25% (1/4) of the capital cost qualifies as Second-Term SUE (where actual SR&ED operating time is >50% in the second period running from acquisition to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months later, totalling up to 50% of the capital cost across both terms). If SUE is later sold or converted to commercial use, ITC recapture is limited to the lesser of the SUE ITCs obtained and the ITC rate applied to 25% or 50% of the proceeds/FMV.

Crucially, under subsection 2900(11) of the Income Tax Regulations, property is disqualified from SUE as a Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) and earns 0% ITC if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended both: (1) that the equipment would be used for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a facility, plant, or line for commercial manufacturing, commercial processing, or another commercial purpose; and (2) that the equipment would be used during its operating time over its expected useful life primarily for non-SR&ED commercial purposes. Equipment used in dedicated non-commercial pilot plants is not considered PDP.
C. Equipment Lease Expenditures (Post-December 15, 2024)

Under the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026), lease payments that first become payable after December 15, 2024 for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada qualify based on the claimant's overhead election and operating time across the entire taxation year (or after December 15, 2024 for a straddle year). Under the Proxy Method, if leased equipment (excluding GPOEF such as desks, chairs, lamps, filing cabinets, photocopiers, fax machines, telephones, cell phones, and calculators—note that computers, hardware, software, and ancillary equipment are not GPOEF) is used ≥90% (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED, 100% of the lease cost may be claimed (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)); if used >50% and <90% (primarily) for SR&ED, 50% of the lease cost may be claimed (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)); if used ≤50%, 0% is claimable. Under the Traditional Method, if leased equipment is used ≥90% (ASA) for SR&ED, 100% is claimed as a lease cost; if used <90% for SR&ED, the proportional percentage used for SR&ED is claimable as overhead on Line 360 of Form T661 if directly related and incremental under Regulation 2900(2)(c) (including leased GPOEF and leased land, whereas building rent remains excluded under both methods unless it is a prescribed special-purpose building under Regulation 2903).
5. Administrative Procedures, Pre-Claim Approval, Filing Deadlines, and Audits
5.1 Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval process (utilizing Form T1322), enabling eligible businesses to obtain an upfront technical determination from the CRA on whether their planned projects meet the definition of SR&ED before starting work or incurring project costs. To qualify for pre-claim approval, the business must: (1) operate in Canada as a CCPC, other Canadian corporation, or partnership; (2) have annual gross business income of less than $25 million; and (3) be in good standing with the CRA. Furthermore, the proposed project must address a scientific or technological uncertainty via a systematic investigation, must not have been included in a previous SR&ED claim, and must not involve issues currently under objection or litigation.
The Pre-Claim Approval workflow follows five sequential steps:

items: Request a Case Number: The business confirms eligibility on Canada.ca and requests a case number (existing SR&ED claimants receive a case number in My Business Account within 2 business days; new claimants receive a phone call from the CRA within 5 business days; businesses may also book one-on-one info sessions by emailing OESCPB-SVEDGPO@cra-arc.gc.ca).
Submit Application via My Business Account: The applicant completes the application using existing project plans and supporting documentation for up to 3 projects.

Meet With an Assigned Research and Technology Advisor (RTA): The CRA assigns an RTA. New claimants have a mandatory 2-to-5-hour virtual or on-site meeting with the RTA (optional for existing claimants in good standing) to discuss the technological baseline, uncertainty, initial hypothesis, and planned experimental protocols.

Receive Written Determination Within 8 Weeks: Within 8 weeks of submitting a completed application, the RTA issues a written Pre-Claim Approval Evaluation Report confirming whether pre-claim approval is granted (valid for up to 3 years unless material project changes occur).

Submit Post-Work Form T661 Claim for Accelerated 90-Day Processing: After undertaking the work, the claimant files Form T661 entering the pre-claim approval case number. Claims containing only pre-approved projects that are selected for an expenditure review benefit from processing service standards cut in half from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days. If pre-claim approval is not granted, the claimant may still undertake the work and file a regular SR&ED claim.

body.text: 5.2 Mandatory Prescribed Forms and 2026 Form T661 Updates

Under the SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (updated January 28, 2025) and the CRA's May 2026 form releases, a compliant SR&ED claim requires filing specific prescribed forms. Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, updated May 15, 2026) comprises 10 parts:

items: Part 1 (General Information) & Part 2 (Project Information, Sections A to C): Part 2 captures technical project descriptions, Canadian Research and Development Classification (CRDC) research codes, pre-claim approval case numbers, and Line 262 (the names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED depreciable properties acquired after December 15, 2024 used in each project, matching Line 390). While a claimant may elect to submit Part 2 descriptions at filing for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value, the costs of every claimed project must be reported in Part 6, and completed Part 2 descriptions for all projects must be maintained at the claimant's place of business and provided to the CRA upon request (failure to provide them results in disallowance of the project's expenditures).

Part 3 (Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures), Part 4 (Qualified Expenditures for ITC), and Part 5 (Prescribed Proxy Amount): Capture the Section 37 pool (including Line 300/306 wages, Line 360 traditional overhead, Line 390 capital expenditures, Line 440 proceeds of disposition of SR&ED capital property, and Line 450 prior-year pool balance), the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool (including Line 502 PPA, Line 504 SUE, Lines 513/514 provincial government assistance, Line 535/540 NAL transfers, Line 557 current SR&ED expenditures, and Line 559 total qualified expenditures), and the Part 5 PPA salary base calculation.

Part 6 (Project Costs — Expanded in May 2026): Part 6A reports project-by-project costs for all projects. Part 6B (Capital Expenditures) requires reporting up to the 20 most expensive capital expenditures for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 across Box 780 (property name matching Line 262), Box 782 (full capital cost including purchase price, installation, customs/excise duties, and transportation), and Box 786 (project numbers). Part 6C (Shared-Use Equipment) requires reporting up to the 20 most expensive SUE expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024 across Box 788 (SUE property name), Box 790 (purchase date in YYYY-MM-DD format), Box 792 (25% of capital cost), Box 794 (1 for First-Term SUE or 2 for Second-Term SUE), and Box 796 (project numbers).

Parts 7, 8, 9, and 10: Part 7 captures additional statistics, and Part 8 contains the claim checklist (Lines 270–282 supporting evidence indicators). Part 9 (Claim Preparer Information) mandates full disclosure of any claim preparer who accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the claim and their billing arrangement; while Part 9 is not subject to the 18-month disallowance deadline, missing, incomplete, or inaccurate Part 9 information triggers a $1,000 penalty for which the claimant and claim preparer are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable. Part 10 contains the signing officer's certification.

5.3 The Absolute 18-Month Reporting Deadline and Audit Dispute Resolution
A. Statutory Reporting Bar (Subsections 37(11), 127(9)(m), and 220(2.2))

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, a taxpayer must file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) containing the prescribed information on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year. For corporations (whose T2 filing-due date is 6 months after taxation year-end), the SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of the taxation year. For individuals carrying on a business (whose T1 filing-due date is June 15 of the following year), the reporting deadline is 17.5 months after the December 31 year-end (June 15 plus 12 months). If the reporting deadline falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or CRA-recognized public holiday, the claim is on time if received or postmarked on or before the next business day.

Pursuant to subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act, the Minister has zero statutory discretion to waive or extend the SR&ED reporting deadline under subsection 220(2.1) taxpayer relief provisions. If the CRA reviews a claim filed before the reporting deadline and identifies deficiencies, the CRA cannot grant additional time past the 18-month reporting deadline to fix them. Under the CRA's partial disallowance policy, if a claimant claims 15 projects in Part 6 but submits Part 2 project information for only 10 projects before the 18-month deadline, the 10 complete projects will be accepted and the 5 incomplete projects will be permanently disallowed.
B. The CRA Review Process, Dispute Escalation, and Gross Negligence Penalties

Under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026) and Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns (updated December 5, 2025), the CRA aims to process refundable SR&ED claims within 180 calendar days of receiving a complete claim (90 calendar days for expenditure-only reviews of pre-claim approved projects), whereas non-refundable claims selected for review have no service standard. Once a claim is selected for review, it cannot be withdrawn, and Part 10 certification cannot be revoked. While oral interviews with technical personnel are part of the RTA's review, oral statements do not replace contemporaneous written or physical documentation. Under Application Policy SR&ED 95-04R, if the CRA retains an outside technical consultant, the consultant must declare any conflict of interest, and the claimant has the right to review the consultant's CV and request reassignment if a conflict exists.
If disagreements arise during a review, claimants must follow three sequential administrative steps before the file is closed:

items: Step 1: Discuss concerns directly with the assigned Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and/or Financial Reviewer (FR).
Step 2: Escalate unresolved issues to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM).

Step 3 — Request an Administrative Review (Form RC532): After receiving the CRA's 30-day Proposal Package and before the file is closed, the claimant may submit Form RC532 to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre (Business Tax Incentives Directorate, 427 Laurier Ave W, Ottawa, ON K1A 0L5). Forwarded within 3 business days to the local SR&ED Assistant Director, the Administrative Review is not a second technical review, but evaluates whether the review complied with current SR&ED legislation and policies and whether the claimant was afforded due process.

body.text: If a reassessment is issued, the claimant may file a formal Notice of Objection to the CRA Appeals Branch, followed by an appeal to the Tax Court of Canada. Conversely, under the Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025), if the CRA proves on a balance of probabilities that a claimant knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence made a false statement or omission on an original or amended SR&ED claim, subsection 163(2) imposes a civil penalty equal to the greater of $100 and 50% of the understated Part I tax payable and/or overstated refundable ITC (computed by treating overstated SR&ED deductions and ITCs as deducted first, without offset by discretionary CCA).
6. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Government Assistance Grinding
6.1 Government Assistance Grinding Mechanics (Subsections 37(1)(d) and 127(18)–(20))

Under subsection 127(9), paragraph 37(1)(d), and subsections 127(18) to 127(20) of the Income Tax Act, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (as well as direct federal, provincial, or municipal R&D grants, subsidies, and forgivable loans) constitute "government assistance". Government assistance that a claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before its income tax return filing-due date reduces both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool on a project-by-project basis (reducing project expenditures to nil, with any excess assistance included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x)).

Consequently, federal and provincial R&D tax credits are not simply summed; the provincial credit reduces ("grinds") the federal qualified expenditure base on which the 35% or 15% federal ITC is computed:

Net Federal Qualified Expenditures = Gross Qualified Expenditures − Provincial/Territorial R&D Tax Credits and Other Government Assistance; Federal ITC = 35% or 15% × Net Federal Qualified Expenditures

Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, government assistance does not reduce the salary base used to compute the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA); rather, the assistance is deducted from total qualified expenditures after the 55% PPA has been added.
6.2 Québec: The Consolidated CRIC Regime (Effective After March 25, 2025)

In the Québec Budget of March 25, 2025 (detailed in Revenu Québec Tax News of July 9, 2025 and official Gouvernement du Québec guidance updated July 7, 2026), Québec enacted a sweeping overhaul of its provincial innovation tax system. For taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec eliminated seven legacy innovation tax measures and replaced them with the consolidated Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation — CRIC).
A. Eliminated Legacy Québec Tax Measures (Tax Years Beginning After March 25, 2025)

As confirmed by Revenu Québec, the following legacy measures were eliminated for taxation years or partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025 (remaining claimable only for taxation years beginning before March 26, 2025): (1) the tax credit for salaries and wages of researchers (R&D); (2) the tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or a research consortium; (3) the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium; (4) the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research; (5) the tax credit for technological adaptation services; (6) the industrial design component of the design tax credits (while the fashion design component remains eligible); and (7) the tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts.
B. CRIC Rates, Pre-Commercialization Expansion, Capital Property, and Exclusion Threshold

Unlike the former Québec R&D wage credit (which varied from 14% to 30% based on corporate asset size), the CRIC provides a two-tier, 100% refundable tax credit to any eligible corporation (or member of a qualified partnership) operating a business with an establishment in Québec, regardless of asset size:

items: 30% refundable rate on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding the applicable exclusion threshold; and
20% refundable rate on all qualified expenditures exceeding the initial $1,000,000 maximum.

body.text: The CRIC covers two distinct activity streams carried out in Québec. First, R&D activities (basic research, applied research, and experimental development) are fully harmonized with the federal subsection 248(1) definition, with scientific reviews conducted by the CRA. Second, pre-commercialization activities—which must be undertaken in Québec in conjunction with and as a continuation of R&D work carried out in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation—cover tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements for obtaining an initial approval or certification (including implementing a quality control system required for initial certification), as well as product design (development of form and aesthetics, improved functionality, prototype development, pilot user validation, and choice of materials).

Qualified expenditures under the CRIC comprise: (1) 100% of salaries and wages paid to employees for eligible R&D and pre-commercialization work in Québec; (2) 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for eligible work carried out in Québec; (3) 50% of payments made to an eligible Québec public research centre, research consortium, or university entity; and (4) 100% of property acquisition costs for capital equipment used in eligible R&D or pre-commercialization in Québec (excluding land, buildings, rights to use land or buildings, and property used in a certified Large Investment Project tax holiday). A corporation cannot claim both the CRIC and another Québec tax credit (such as the C3i investment and innovation credit) on the same expenditure.

Before the 30% and 20% rates apply, a corporation's qualified expenditures must exceed an annual exclusion threshold equal to the greater of: (1) $50,000; or (2) the sum of the basic personal amount (BPA) of the Québec personal income tax system for each eligible employee, adjusted to reflect the percentage of time spent by each employee on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities. Practitioner guides report the Québec BPA per full-time eligible employee as $18,571 for 2025 and $18,952 for 2026. For example, if a Québec corporation in 2026 employs 25 full-time R&D engineers incurring $1,500,000 in eligible salaries and equipment costs, its employee exclusion threshold is 25 × $18,952 = $473,800 (exceeding the $50,000 minimum). Subtracting $473,800 from $1,500,000 leaves $1,026,200 in net qualified expenditures, generating a CRIC refund of (30% × $1,000,000) + (20% × $26,200) = $305,240 (note that an industry blog example miscalculated $1,500,000 minus 25 × $18,952 as $1,144,650 due to an arithmetic typo).

To claim the CRIC, corporations file Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (and Form RD-1029.8.CR) alongside Form RD-222-V (Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures) with their Québec corporate return. Additionally, for Québec's Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (DCI), the Québec nexus ratio for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 is calculated using R&D expenditures eligible for the CRIC (without reduction by the exclusion threshold), while excluding pre-commercialization expenditures.
6.3 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, OBRITC, and 2026 Capital Expenditure Harmonization

Ontario administers three corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) through the CRA via the T2 Corporation Income Tax Return. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule 566) provides an 8% refundable tax credit to qualifying corporations on up to $3,000,000 of annual qualified SR&ED expenditures performed in Ontario (a maximum annual refund of $240,000). The $3,000,000 expenditure limit is shared among associated corporations and phases out when prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, or when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000.

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508, Sections 38–45) provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit on eligible SR&ED expenditures carried on in Ontario (reduced by any OITC and other government assistance, unless waived under subsection 43(1)), with a 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Schedules 568 and 569) provides a 20% refundable tax credit on up to $20,000,000 of qualified current expenditures (a maximum $4,000,000 annual credit) incurred under an eligible contract with an eligible Ontario research institute (universities, colleges, hospital research institutes, or Ontario Centres of Excellence).

Because Ontario's OITC and ORDTC cross-reference section 127 of the federal Income Tax Act, the restoration of 100% of qualified capital expenditures and lease costs made on or after December 16, 2024 took effect automatically in Ontario when federal Bill C-15 received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, as confirmed on Ontario.ca and in the 2026 Ontario Economic Outlook and Fiscal Review / Fall Statement.
6.4 British Columbia, Alberta, and Other Provincial/Territorial Regimes

In British Columbia, Budget 2026 (Bill 2, Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026) made the BC SR&ED Tax Credit (Form T666, Part 6 of the BC Income Tax Act) permanent and aligned it with federal Bill C-15 effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Qualifying CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) with a BC permanent establishment may claim a 10% refundable tax credit on up to the increased $6,000,000 expenditure limit (yielding up to $600,000 in refundable BC credits), phased out over prior-year taxable capital (or 3-year average gross revenue) between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000. Qualifying corporations with BC expenditures above the refundable limit (or non-CCPC/non-ECPC corporations and active partnership members) earn a 10% non-refundable tax credit (with a 3-year carryback and 10-year carryforward), and capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024 are restored as BC qualified expenditures. Form T666 must be filed within 18 months of the taxation year-end.

In Alberta, Treasury Board and Finance administers the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG — AT1 Schedule 29 / Form AT29) under Division 7 of Part 6 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act, Information Circular IEG-1R5, and Special Notice Vol. 8 No. 9 (both updated June 30, 2026 following Bill C-15). The IEG provides a refundable tax credit on up to $4,000,000 in annual Alberta R&D spending (phased out between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year federal taxable capital): an 8% base payment on eligible spending up to the corporation's base spending level (its average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding 2 taxation years), plus an additional 12% payment (for a combined 20% rate) on eligible spending exceeding that 2-year average base. Crucially, per the June 30, 2026 updated Alberta IEG Guide, for taxation years ending after December 15, 2024, the IEG is computed using the federal amount of current SR&ED expenditures reported at Line 557 of Form T661 (rather than Line 559 total qualified expenditures used for tax years ending before December 16, 2024), and the resulting IEG must be reported as provincial government assistance on Line 513 of federal Form T661.

body.text: 6.5 Worked Numerical Example: Integrated Federal + Provincial Stacking and Grinding (2026)

To illustrate the exact statutory interaction between restored capital expenditures, the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount, provincial tax credit grinding, and the split 100% / 40% federal refundability rules, consider an Ontario-based Qualifying CCPC with a December 31, 2026 taxation year-end, prior-year taxable income of $300,000, and prior-year taxable capital of $8,000,000 (below both the federal $15 million threshold and Ontario's $25 million threshold). During 2026, the corporation elects the Proxy Method and incurs $1,000,000 in direct hands-on SR&ED salaries (no specified employees) and acquires $200,000 in new depreciable laboratory testing equipment after December 15, 2024 used 100% (ASA) for SR&ED in Ontario:

items: Step 1 — Calculate Un-Ground Federal Qualified Expenditures: Direct SR&ED salaries ($1,000,000) plus new SR&ED capital equipment acquired after December 15, 2024 ($200,000) plus the Prescribed Proxy Amount at 55% of the $1,000,000 salary base under Regulation 2900(4) ($550,000) yield $1,750,000 in Total Un-Ground Qualified Expenditures (comprising $1,550,000 in current qualified expenditures and $200,000 in capital qualified expenditures).

Step 2 — Calculate Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule 566): Because Ontario restored 100% of post-December 15, 2024 qualified capital expenditures upon Royal Assent of Bill C-15, the full $1,750,000 is eligible for the 8% OITC (under the $3,000,000 limit), yielding an OITC of $140,000 (8% × $1,750,000, fully refundable; attributable $124,000 to current expenditures and $16,000 to capital expenditures).

Step 3 — Calculate Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508): The $140,000 OITC is government assistance that reduces the expenditure pool for the 3.5% ORDTC to $1,610,000 ($1,750,000 − $140,000), yielding a non-refundable ORDTC of $56,350 (3.5% × $1,610,000; attributable $49,910 to current expenditures and $6,440 to capital expenditures).

Step 4 — Calculate Net Federal Qualified Expenditures (After Provincial Grinding): Total Ontario government assistance is $140,000 + $56,350 = $196,350. Subtracting this assistance yields Net Federal Current Qualified Expenditures of $1,376,090 ($1,550,000 − $173,910) and Net Federal Capital Qualified Expenditures of $177,560 ($200,000 − $22,440), for Total Net Federal Qualified Expenditures of $1,553,650 (well within the $6,000,000 expenditure limit).

Step 5 — Calculate Federal 35% SR&ED ITC and Cash Refundability: The Federal ITC on Current Expenditures is 35% × $1,376,090 = $481,631.50 (which is 100% refundable = $481,631.50 cash refund if no Part I tax is payable). The Federal ITC on Capital Expenditures is 35% × $177,560 = $62,146.00 (which is 40% refundable = $24,858.40 cash refund, with the remaining $37,287.60 available to offset Part I tax or carry back 3 / forward 20 years). Total combined federal and Ontario credits equal $740,127.50 on $1,200,000 of actual cash outlays (a 61.68% total recovery rate).

body.text: 7. Direct Federal R&D Grants, Ecosystem Programs, and Policy Outlook
7.1 NRC IRAP (2026 Streams, SDTC Integration, and CIC Transition)

The National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) is Canada's primary direct R&D grant program for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs with 1 to 500 employees). As documented in program guides, NRC IRAP provides expert technical and business advisory services through Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs) alongside non-repayable financial contributions reimbursing 60% to 80% of internal technical salaries (and a portion of Canadian arm's-length contractor fees) for R&D projects, while excluding general overhead, rent, travel, and capital equipment. Typical SME project grants range from $50,000 to $500,000 over 12 to 24 months, while large-scale strategic streams support awards up to $10,000,000.
In 2026, NRC IRAP operates five distinct funding streams:

items: Core IRAP: Flagship non-repayable R&D contributions and ITA advisory services across all technology sectors.

Clean Technology Assistance Stream (CTAS — Absorbing SDTC): Following the federal government's June 2024 wind-down of Sustainable Development Technology Canada (SDTC), SDTC stopped signing new funding agreements and its cleantech mandate (along with approximately $98 million in cleantech funding) transitioned into NRC IRAP's Clean Technology stream, with existing project transfers concluding in spring 2025 and the CTAS intake live for 2025–2026.

Defence Industry Assist (DI Assist): Launched in January 2026 with $244.2 million in federal funding to support SMEs developing dual-use technologies with both civilian and defence applications for the Canadian Armed Forces.

AI Assist Program: Supported by $100 million over five years to help SMEs build and deploy artificial intelligence capabilities, complementing Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada's (ISED) $2 billion Canadian Sovereign AI Compute Strategy launched in December 2024.
Youth Employment Program: Provides wage subsidies for SMEs to hire recent graduates.

body.text: With respect to the Canada Innovation Corporation (CIC), on December 19, 2023, the Government of Canada announced that the establishment of the CIC and the transition of NRC IRAP into the CIC will take place no later than 2026–2027. Pending that launch, NRC IRAP continues to operate directly within the National Research Council throughout 2026.
7.2 Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF), Mitacs, NSERC, and Stacking With SR&ED

ISED's Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) invests in large-scale innovative R&D, commercialization, and industrial transformation projects across Canada. Under the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, both non-repayable SIF grants and conditionally repayable SIF contributions (where repayments are contingent solely on earning future profits or revenues from the project rather than firm, unconditional terms of repayment) are treated by the CRA as government assistance under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 12(1)(x), reducing the Section 37 and Section 127 SR&ED pools when received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received (and generating SR&ED pool additions/ITCs only if and when actually repaid).

Similarly, direct R&D wage grants from NRC IRAP, Mitacs, and NSERC Alliance (as well as historical Canada Emergency Wage Subsidy (CEWS) and Temporary Wage Subsidy (TWS) receipts for employees performing SR&ED) constitute government assistance that grinds deductible and qualified SR&ED expenditures on a project-by-project basis. However, because government assistance does not reduce the salary base used to calculate the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount under Regulation 2900(4), stacking NRC IRAP with SR&ED remains highly beneficial: on $100,000 of direct SR&ED wages under the proxy method ($100,000 salary + $55,000 PPA = $155,000 gross qualified expenditures), an $80,000 NRC IRAP grant leaves $75,000 of net qualified expenditures eligible for the 35% federal ITC ($26,250), yielding $106,250 in combined IRAP and SR&ED support.
7.3 Status of the Proposed Federal Patent Box Regime

The Department of Finance Canada conducted a public consultation on creating a federal Patent Box regime to encourage intellectual property retention and commercialization in Canada, which closed on April 15, 2024, alongside proposals for an innovation-focused flow-through share regime. However, both the federal patent box regime and the innovation flow-through share regime were absent from Federal Budget 2025 (November 4, 2025) and Bill C-15, and the federal government has provided no indication of whether those proposals have been deferred or abandoned. Consequently, patent box incentives in Canada currently exist solely at the provincial level (such as Québec's Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (DCI)).
8. Landmark Canadian Case Law and Audit Precedents

Canadian courts have established an extensive body of jurisprudence interpreting subsection 248(1), section 37, and section 127 of the Income Tax Act. The table and case analyses below synthesize the controlling judicial precedents governing CRA audits and Tax Court appeals through October 2026.
